In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental issue in the debate over merit pay: whether the system is inherently demoralizing to teachers.
the question of whether teachers in general are likely to be supportive or hostile to the idea of merit pay.
the question of whether merit pay is an appropriate means of improving teacher effectiveness and student learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
teachers in general do not oppose merit pay, and that teachers who teach the most disadvantaged and low-attaining children are not more likely to oppose merit pay than are others.
merit pay is not universally unpopular among teachers.
merit pay is not a divisive issue among teachers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the attitudes of public school teachers toward merit pay are generally positive, and the attitudes of private school teachers are even more positive.
teachers are generally supportive of the idea of merit pay, but that they are less supportive of specific proposals to implement it.
teachers in merit pay districts do not appear to be alienated from the system, but rather, they are generally positive about it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
merit pay may be a viable option for improving teacher quality and student achievement, especially in districts that have been unable to attract and retain high-quality teachers.
merit pay is not a panacea but is one of several possible strategies for improving teacher quality and school effectiveness.
merit pay is not the "poison" that some have made it out to be.
